h1: Leather and tobacco notes in long aged strong ales
title: Leather and Tobacco Notes in Aged Ales | Craft Beer School
desc: Why long aged barleywines, old ales and imperial stouts can taste of leather and tobacco, where the notes come from and when they turn bad.
teaser: Leather and tobacco in a ten year old barleywine can be magic. Too much and it tastes like an old shoe in a damp cupboard.
standfirst: Leather and tobacco are flavours of long ageing. They appear in strong ales that have spent years in the bottle and in some beers touched by Brettanomyces or wood. In balance they add depth. Out of balance they bury everything else. Here is how to tell which.
sections: What leather and tobacco taste like

Leather in beer is the smell of a well-worn leather armchair, a saddle or a new pair of shoes: dry, slightly animal and rich. Tobacco ranges from dry pipe tobacco and cigar box to the sweeter smell of tobacco leaf. In an aged strong ale they often sit alongside sherry, dried fruit, toffee, soy sauce or old wood. Bitterness is usually low and the beer tastes round and mellow.

These notes rarely show in young beer. They develop slowly over years, which is why they are most familiar to people who cellar beer or taste vintage bottles.

Three sources usually overlap:

  • Slow oxidation. The beer flavour wheel lists leathery among the stale flavours, alongside papery and catty. In a strong, dark beer, slow oxidation over years produces leathery and tobacco notes rather than plain cardboard.
  • Brettanomyces. This wild yeast produces 4-ethylphenol and 4-ethylguaiacol, which give leather, horse blanket, smoke and clove. Bottles with Brett in them, deliberately or not, often turn leathery with age. Our guide to Brettanomyces covers it.
  • Wood. Beer aged in oak barrels can pick up tobacco and cigar box notes from the wood, particularly from casks that previously held whisky, sherry or wine.

Leather and tobacco suit beers that are strong, dark and built to age:

  • Barleywine, especially English style, after several years
  • Old ale and stock ale
  • Imperial stout, particularly barrel-aged versions
  • Belgian quadrupel and strong dark ale
  • Some wild and Brett-aged strong ales

Most of these sit at 8 to 12% ABV. Alcohol and rich malt give the beer enough body to carry the darker, drier notes. Our guide to sherry and raisin notes in aged beer covers the dried fruit stage that usually comes first.

Leather and tobacco are welcome in moderation. They become faults when:

  • They dominate so completely that malt and fruit disappear.
  • They show up in a pale or hoppy beer, where they mean staling or contamination.
  • They come with wet cardboard, soy sauce or musty notes that point to a beer past its peak or stored badly.
  • A clean beer that was never meant to have Brett turns leathery and phenolic, which suggests contamination.

A useful test is to ask whether the leather adds depth to the beer or replaces it. If you can still find malt sweetness, dried fruit and a balanced finish, the note is working.
Telling Brett leather from age leather

Leather from Brett and leather from oxidation can taste similar, but they usually travel with different companions. Brett leather tends to come with smoke, clove, horse blanket or a farmyard edge. The beer is often drier than expected because Brett keeps fermenting sugars that brewing yeast left behind. A bottle with Brett may also be more highly carbonated than it was when young, which is worth knowing before you open one.

Leather from slow oxidation comes with sherry, toffee, dried fruit and sometimes soy sauce. Sweetness and body stay roughly where they were while bitterness fades. If a strong ale has turned leathery and also thin, dry and fizzy, Brett is the likelier cause. If it is leathery, sweet and sherried, age is doing the work. Neither is automatically good or bad. What matters is whether the result fits the beer.
Cellaring for good leather, not bad

If you want to age strong beer at home:

  1. Choose a strong, dark beer built to age.
  2. Store bottles upright, in the dark, at a cool, steady temperature, ideally around 10 to 14 °C.
  3. Avoid temperature swings. A cupboard on an outside wall can swing by many degrees in a day.
  4. Buy several bottles and open one every year or two.
  5. Keep notes so you can see when the beer peaks.

In India, steady cool storage is the hard part. Many homes have no cellar and summer room temperatures are above 30 °C. A wine fridge set to about 12 °C is the simplest answer for anyone serious about ageing. Beer kept warm tends to go straight to stale without passing through the pleasant leather and tobacco stage.

Serve aged strong ales a little warmer than lagers, around 12 to 14 °C, in a glass with a wide bowl so the aromas gather. Pour small measures, because these beers are strong. Keep water on the table. Taste slowly and let the beer warm in the glass. Leather and tobacco often open up after a few minutes.

Your first step: buy two bottles of the same English style barleywine, drink one now with notes and put the other away somewhere cool and dark for two years.
faqs: Why does aged beer taste of leather?
Slow oxidation over years, Brettanomyces producing 4-ethylphenol or contact with oak barrels can all give leather notes.
Is leather flavour in beer a fault?
Not in a long aged strong ale, where it can add depth. In a pale or hoppy beer it usually signals staling or contamination.
Strong, dark beers built to age, such as barleywine, old ale, imperial stout and quadrupel, especially barrel-aged versions.
What temperature should I cellar strong beer at?
Cool, dark and steady, ideally around 10 to 14 °C, with as little day to night variation as you can manage.
